analysis.one_liner: Caps what insured patients pay out of pocket for a drug at the drug's average cash price.
analysis.headline: The Fair Prescription Pricing Act was introduced in the House with no cosponsors and referred to three committees, where no vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar group health plans and health insurers from charging a patient more in copays, coinsurance, or deductibles for a prescription drug than the drug's nationwide average cash purchase price. It applies the same rule to pharmacy benefit managers, the middlemen that set drug benefits for insurers and employers. The upshot: a patient would never pay more out of pocket than the drug actually costs on the open market.
analysis.who_benefits: Insured patients who fill prescriptions, especially people on high-deductible plans who can currently be charged a copay or coinsurance amount larger than the drug's actual cash price. The bill says plans and insurers must make sure any pharmacy benefit manager they use follows the same cap.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Public Health Service Act, ERISA, and the tax code to prohibit group health plans and health insurers from imposing cost sharing (deductibles, coinsurance, copayments) on a covered outpatient drug dispensed at an in-network pharmacy in an amount exceeding the nationwide average of consumer purchase prices for that drug over the prior year. [S2]

The cap is calculated using data from the Medicaid drug price survey described in section 1927(f)(1)(A)(i) of the Social Security Act, so the benchmark is an actual surveyed market price rather than a plan's own numbers. [S2]

Each version of the rule states that plans and issuers must ensure any pharmacy benefit manager providing services under the plan complies with the cap in the same manner as the plan or issuer, closing the route around the cap through middlemen. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and health insurers, who would give up cost-sharing revenue that today can exceed what the drug actually costs. Employers sponsoring plans face a compliance duty, though the cap may also lower what their employees pay.

drawbacks.text: Cost sharing is one lever plans use to hold premiums down; capping it at the cash price could push more costs into monthly premiums, which people who don't fill many prescriptions would feel. [S2]

The cap only covers drugs dispensed at in-network pharmacies, so patients who use an out-of-network pharmacy get no protection, and the bill does nothing about the underlying list prices drug manufacturers charge. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit to patients is concrete: no one's copay would exceed the drug's actual market price, which mainly fixes the specific case where middlemen mark up what a patient owes beyond the drug's cost. The trade-off is that the money has to come from somewhere — premiums, plan design, or lower payments to intermediaries — and the bill leaves that distribution unstated. It is a narrow fix, not a broad drug-price overhaul.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was just introduced in late August 2026 and sent to three House committees; it has no cosponsors and no hearings or votes scheduled yet.

narrative.text: Rep. Hillary Scholten introduced the Fair Prescription Pricing Act of 2026 in the House on August 20, 2026. [S1]

The same day, the bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, and additionally to the Ways and Means and Education and Workforce Committees, for consideration of provisions within their jurisdictions. [S4]
The bill has zero cosponsors, so no other member has signed on in support. [S3]
No further action — no committee vote, hearing record, or floor consideration — appears in the bill's action history. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: At this point, no one has won or lost; the status quo stands, and pharmacy benefit managers and insurers continue collecting cost sharing that can exceed a drug's cash price while the bill sits without cosponsors or a scheduled vote.

for.name: Rep. Hillary Scholten
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and saw it referred to three committees; so far its only supporter in Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only one member, a Democrat, has taken a position; no Republican or Democratic cosponsors, and no opposition is on the record.

industries.note: The bill says plans must make PBMs comply with the same cost-sharing cap, ending the practice of charging patients more than the drug's cash price — often called spread pricing, where the middleman keeps the difference. PBMs' margin on patient cost sharing would shrink. [S2]

Insurers would have to police the cap for themselves and their PBM contractors, giving up cost-sharing revenue that today can exceed a drug's actual cost. Some of that cost may shift to premiums, which spreads it back to all enrollees. [S2]
ERISA plans face a new compliance duty, but employees' out-of-pocket drug costs would fall, which employers often share through healthier workforces and lower premium pressure. [S2]

analysis.trajectory: With a single sponsor, zero cosponsors, and a three-committee referral in the final months of a two-year Congress, the bill is very unlikely to get a committee hearing or floor vote; most bills at this stage die quietly when the Congress ends in January 2027.
